p144.lead: Retirement on Mount Gilboa and quiet work in the Decapolis: the discourse on prayer, the believer’s prayer and seven specimen prayers, the conference with John’s apostles, and the death of John the Baptist.

p144.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p144.s0.h: Introduction — Quiet Preparation Before the Public Ministry
p144.s0.b0: In September and October of A.D. 27, Jesus and the apostles lived at a secluded camp on the slopes of Mount Gilboa. The Jerusalem leaders were hostile, Herod Antipas held John in prison and was suspicious of his connection with Jesus, and tension was growing between John’s disciples and Jesus’ apostles. These three circumstances led to the retirement.
p144.s0.b1: Jesus knew that the days of preliminary work were nearly over. He wanted to begin the final effort of his life, but in a way that would cause John the Baptist no pain or embarrassment. So he chose to train the apostles while awaiting John’s fate. This is also the paper that treats the subject of prayer most deeply.
p144.s1.h: I. The Gilboa Encampment — Three Reasons for Retirement

head: Reason for retirement
Content
rows: To confirm their understanding of, and faith in, the gospel of the kingdom
To allow opposition in Judea and Galilee to quiet down
To await the fate of John the Baptist

p144.s1.b1: The apostles’ devotion still rested mainly on personal loyalty; they had not yet grasped the full meaning of Jesus’ teaching and bestowal. They also differed about the kingdom: John and Andrew held that it had already come, Peter and James that it had not yet come, while the twins remained serene, hardly aware of the debate. Jesus spent most of this time alone on the mountain.
p144.s1.b2: The text says that what Jesus did in those hours, after the forty days following his baptism, is better called personal communion with the Father than prayer or worship. Through September the discussions centered on prayer and worship, until at last Thomas asked, “⟦Q 144:1.9⟧Master, teach us how to pray.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus did not favor set forms of prayer, but since the common people needed a simple prayer, he granted the request.
p144.s2.h: II. The Discourse on Prayer — The Breath of the Soul
p144.s2.b0: Jesus said that the short prayer John had taught was meant for the multitude, not as a mold into which the apostles should pour their own souls. Then he defined what prayer is.

p144.s2.b1.q: Prayer is entirely a personal and spontaneous expression of the attitude of the soul toward the spirit

p144.s2.b2: With the stories of the friend who went at midnight to borrow bread and the widow who kept coming to the unjust judge, Jesus taught persistence. But he made it clear that these stories did not mean petitions can change the Father. Even when his children ask foolishly, the Father gives what is fitting, not a stone or a serpent.

p144.s2.b3.q: Your persistence, however, is not to win favor with God but to change your earth attitude and to enlarge your soul’s capacity for spirit receptivity.

p144.s2.b4: This passage matters especially for readers discouraged by unanswered prayer. The first fruit of prayer is not getting what we want but becoming a larger vessel for receiving the spirit. Jesus added that people exercise too little faith when they pray.
p144.s3.h: III. The Believer’s Prayer — The Prayer of the Nazareth Home
p144.s3.b0: James Zebedee wanted a form of prayer to teach new believers, not the apostles themselves. Jesus offered the prayer he had taught his brothers and sisters in Nazareth. He always taught that one should pray in secret, he was reluctant to pray in public, and he never taught a form of individual prayer, only group or family prayers.

p144.s3.b1.q: Refresh our souls with the water of life.

p144.s3.b2: Following the request for tomorrow’s bread, this line asks for food for the soul along with food for the body. The text notes that in later copying two lines were lost and other words added. The closing request, to be made more and more like the Father in perfection, shows that this prayer reaches beyond daily needs toward growth in perfection.

head: Conditions of effective prayer
How the text puts it
rows: In submission to the Father’s all-wise will

p144.s3.b4: In his own all-night prayers on the mountain, Jesus prayed mainly for his disciples and very little for himself. Instead he gave much time to worship of a kind that was understanding communion with the Father.
p144.s4.h: IV. More about Prayer — Batteries and Receivers
p144.s4.b0: Jesus’ answers to the questions that followed for several days are summarized in modern terms. Sincere prayer offered in faith, even for things foolish or impossible to grant directly, never fails to enlarge the soul’s capacity for spiritual receptivity. Sonship is not earned by effort but received as a gift of grace through faith; what a person does achieve is righteousness, the progressive growth of character.

p144.s4.b1.q: Prayer is the breath of the spirit life in the midst of the material civilization of the races of mankind.

head: Image and definition
Prayer
Worship
rows: Recharging the spiritual batteries of the soul
Tuning in the soul to catch the universe broadcasts of the Father’s infinite spirit
The breath of the spirit life amid material civilization
A technique for escaping the monotony of daily routine

p144.s4.b3.q: Prayer is a part of the divine plan for making over that which is into that which ought to be.

p144.s4.b4: Peter, James, and John spent long nights with Jesus without hearing him pray, because most of his praying was done silently, in spirit and mind. His habit shows that prayer is a matter not of the quantity of words but of the soul’s direction.
p144.s5.h: V. Other Forms of Prayer — Seven Specimen Prayers
p144.s5.b0: To illustrate other matters, Jesus presented several more forms of prayer, asking the apostles not to teach these “prayer parables” to the multitude. The text explains that many of them came from other inhabited planets, and that specific permission was granted to transcribe seven of them into this record.

head: How the specimen prayer addresses God
A notable request
rows: The Father in whom the universe realms consist
His nature and character bestowed on us
The creative Parent at the center of the universe
His indwelling, guiding spirit within us
Our perfect and righteous heavenly Father
Guidance on the way of eternal progress
Our Father, who dwells in mystery
The will to walk the path he shows
A glorious Father and Mother in one parent
Love that embraces the weak; patience and kindness
Our all-faithful Source and mighty Center
A mind renewed by the indwelling spirit
Our Father who dwells in the secret places of the universe
Not to be forsaken when the path is hard and dark

p144.s5.b2.q: And give us the will to walk therein.

p144.s5.b3: Different as their wording is, the seven prayers share a common movement. They ask for the Father’s character, seek guidance for today, long to become more and more like him, and hope at last to be received into his arms. The apostles could not teach them publicly, but they profited much from them in their personal religious experience.
p144.s6.h: VI. Conference with John’s Apostles — Learning to Co-operate Without Jesus
p144.s6.b0: A chance meeting in a market in early October led to a three-week conference at Gilboa between Jesus’ twelve apostles and John’s twelve. Jesus firmly declined to take part in the discussions and spoke only three times, on sympathy, co-operation, and tolerance. He said that he would help with personal religious problems as the Father’s representative, but that questions of the socialization of religion they must settle themselves, and he left them for two weeks.

p144.s6.b1.q: I am the representative of the Father to the individual, not to the group.

head: Decision of the conference
Content
rows: Both groups adopted the prayer Jesus had taught as the one to teach believers
While John lived, each group would work separately, meeting jointly for a week every three months
Only John’s apostles would baptize, and Jesus’ apostles would teach: a first step toward outward union
John’s apostles would follow Jesus’ direction, and Jesus’ apostles would begin water baptism as a symbol of the spirit baptism
John’s group: “Repent and be baptized”; Jesus’ group: “Believe and be baptized”

p144.s6.b3: The text calls this the first attempt of Jesus’ followers to socialize their personal religious practice. The twenty-four men disagreed, debated, prayed, and compromised, and learned to tolerate one another’s honest opinions. On his return Jesus promised to help them carry out the spirit of what they had agreed together. His way of leaving a community to settle its own affairs has much to say to communities of faith today.
p144.s7.h: VII–VIII. In the Decapolis Cities; In Camp near Pella — An Answer for John
p144.s7.b0: In November and December Jesus and the twenty-four worked in pairs in Scythopolis, Gerasa, Abila, and Gadara, John’s apostles baptizing and Jesus’ apostles teaching. The text observes that the socialized religion of a new revelation always pays the price of compromise with the forms of earlier religion, and explains that baptism was the price paid for bringing John’s followers along.
p144.s7.b1: At the end of December, at the camp near Pella, messengers came from John in prison to ask whether Jesus was the true Deliverer. Jesus told them to report that John was not forgotten and that the gospel was being preached to the poor. Then he told the crowd that John was asking not from doubt but to reassure his disciples, and that John was no reed shaken by the wind but more than a prophet.

p144.s7.b2.q: among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist; yet he who is but small in the kingdom of heaven is greater

p144.s7.b3: The reason is that even the least in the kingdom knows he has been born of the spirit and has become a son of God. The saying shows that the measure of greatness is not achievement but the awareness of sonship. Jesus then invited all who labor and are heavy laden to come and find rest for their souls.
p144.s8.h: IX. Death of John the Baptist — Now Openly
p144.s8.b0: John was executed by order of Herod Antipas on the evening of January 10, A.D. 28. When his disciples brought the news, Jesus called the twenty-four together, told them to arrange their affairs that night, and declared that the time had come to proclaim the kingdom openly and with power. On the morning of January 13 they set out for Capernaum.

p144.s8.b1.q: The hour has come to proclaim the kingdom openly and with power.

p144.s9.b0: Paper 144 records the quiet preparation just before the public ministry and places prayer at its center. Prayer is not a technique for persuading God; it changes the attitude of the soul and enlarges its capacity to receive the spirit. And having taught them to pray, Jesus stepped back so that his followers could learn to reconcile their opinions and work together.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Pray as a spontaneous expression of the soul rather than set words
The attitude of the soul toward the spirit (144:2.2)
Persist in prayer, expecting a change in yourself more than an answer
Ask not only for yourself but for others
Receive sonship as a gift, not an achievement
Let worship give you breathing room from daily monotony
A technique of escape from routine (144:4.5)
Learn to empathize and compromise with those who differ

p144.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 145, “Four Eventful Days at Capernaum,” Jesus begins his public ministry in earnest at Capernaum.
p145.lead: Four days in Capernaum: a great catch of fish, a Sabbath sermon proclaiming personal religion, 683 healed at sundown, and a Sunday dawn on which Jesus chose his spiritual mission over wonders.

p145.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p145.s0.h: Introduction — On the Threshold of Public Ministry
p145.s0.b0: After John the Baptist had been sent to his death, Jesus and the apostles arrived in Capernaum on the evening of Tuesday, January 13, and as usual made the home of Zebedee in Bethsaida their headquarters. From Wednesday through Friday Jesus instructed the apostles in preparation for their first public preaching tour of Galilee, and through Andrew he arranged to speak in the synagogue on the coming Sabbath. This paper records the many events that crowded into those four days.
p145.s0.b1: Late on Friday evening Jesus’ baby sister, Ruth, secretly came to see him, and the two spent almost an hour together in a boat anchored near the shore. The narrator tells us that Ruth was the only member of the family who believed in the divinity of his mission consistently and unwaveringly from beginning to end, and that she was his chief comfort among his earth family during his trial, rejection, and crucifixion. Set before the dramatic events that follow, this quiet meeting shows how great a comfort steadfast faith can be.
p145.s1.h: I. The Draught of Fishes — A Miracle That Was No Miracle
p145.s1.b0: On Friday morning, when the crowd pressed Jesus to the water’s edge, he stepped into David Zebedee’s boat and went on teaching for more than two hours. That boat, named “Simon,” was Peter’s old fishing vessel, built by Jesus’ own hands. When he had finished, Jesus told the fishermen, who had toiled all night and caught nothing, to put out into the deep and let down their nets, and they took so many fish that three boats were filled almost to sinking. From that day David Zebedee and his associates forsook their nets and followed Jesus.

p145.s1.b1.q: But this was in no sense a miraculous draught of fishes.

p145.s1.b2: The narrator explains that Jesus, a close student of nature and an experienced fisherman, simply directed the men to the place where the fish were usually found at that time of day. Yet his followers always regarded it as a miracle. This short section is a key to the whole paper. People wanted to see miracles even in ordinary events, and Jesus was wary lest that tendency obscure his spiritual mission.
p145.s2.h: II. Afternoon at the Synagogue — From National Religion to Personal Religion
p145.s2.b0: On the Sabbath afternoon Jesus preached on “⟦Q 145:2.1⟧The Will of the Father in Heaven.⟦/Q⟧” At this time more people believed in him in Capernaum than in any other city on earth. The aim of the sermon was to make clear that religion is a personal experience.

p145.s2.b1.q: All these generations have you had a national or racial religion; now have I come to give you a personal religion.

p145.s2.b2: Jesus reminded his hearers that this was not an entirely new idea: Jeremiah and Ezekiel had already pointed the way. The proverb about the fathers eating sour grapes and the children’s teeth being set on edge would no longer hold; the law would be written in men’s hearts; and all would come to know God personally.
p145.s2.b3: Jesus went on to say that once a person discerns this spiritual freedom, the Father wills that he should begin the eternal ascent of the Paradise career. That career consists in the creature’s conscious response to the divine urge of the indwelling spirit to find the Creator, to know God, and to seek to become like him. Personal religion, in the end, is a life that answers day by day to the spirit within.

head: National religion
Personal religion
rows: God loves you—every one of you—as individuals
The fathers’ sins fall on the children
Only the soul that sins shall die; the Father does not punish a believing child for the sins of a nation
A new covenant written in the heart
The progress and enlightenment of the individual

p145.s2.b5: Jesus added that individual members of a family must often suffer the material consequences of group mistakes. Through this sermon the apostles came to see more fully that the gospel of the kingdom is a message directed to the individual, not to the nation. For readers who lean on the faith of a community, the passage invites reflection on what it means to stand before God as one person.

p145.s2.b6.q: Do you not realize that the hope of a better nation—or a better world—is bound up in the progress and enlightenment of the individual?

p145.s3.h: II (continued). After the Sermon — Coincidences Turned into Miracles
p145.s3.b0: As the sermon ended, a young man in the congregation was seized with an epileptic attack and cried out; Jesus took him by the hand, said “⟦Q 145:2.12⟧Come out of it⟦/Q⟧,” and he awoke. The narrator makes clear that he was not possessed by a demon but was a victim of ordinary epilepsy who had been taught that his affliction came from an evil spirit, and that his real healing came only after sundown. Likewise, the malarial fever of Amatha, Peter’s mother-in-law, merely happened to leave her while Jesus stood beside her.

head: Event
What people believed
What the narrator reveals
rows: An experienced fisherman directing them to where the fish were
The young man in the synagogue
A demon cast out and a miraculous cure
Ordinary epilepsy; the real healing came after sundown
The fever happened to leave her; her cure came hours later, after sundown

p145.s3.b2: The narrator calls these cases typical of the way a wonder-seeking generation and a miracle-minded people seized on coincidences as proof that yet another miracle had been wrought. The Sabbath was just the time for such a rumor to spread quickly, and it soon reached the surrounding settlements.
p145.s4.h: III. The Healing at Sundown — Creative Power That Was Not Planned
p145.s4.b0: Because Jewish teaching forbade seeking health on the Sabbath, the sick waited until the sun went down and then streamed toward Zebedee’s home, until almost a thousand people filled the front yard and the road. The narrator says that the power and authority of that afternoon’s sermon had set the stage for this scene, and records the two sayings with which it closed.

p145.s4.b1.q: Hate is the shadow of fear; revenge the mask of cowardice.

p145.s4.b2: The hearers could not forget another saying either: that man is a son of God, not a child of the devil. The narrator adds that this Sabbath was a great day not only in Jesus’ life but in the life of a universe; to all local universe intents and purposes the little city of Capernaum was the real capital of Nebadon. The handful of Jews in the synagogue were not the only beings who heard those words.

p145.s4.b3.q: Man is the son of God, not a child of the devil.

p145.s4.b4: The suffering throng peculiarly touched Jesus’ human heart. Yet he knew he could never build an enduring spiritual movement on purely material wonders, and since Cana it had been his consistent policy not to exhibit his creator prerogatives. In that moment, when divine wisdom and human compassion were interlocked, he sought refuge in appeal to his Father’s will.
p145.s4.b5: Jesus said that, if it were not inconsistent with the Father’s will, he would desire to see his children made whole. His Personalized Thought Adjuster ruled instantly that such an act would not transgress the Father’s will; the celestial retinue descended, and in a moment 683 men, women, and children were healed. The narrator says that no such mass physical healing took place on earth before or after, and that of all who witnessed it, Jesus himself was the most surprised.

p145.s4.b6.q: What a Creator Son desires and his Father wills IS.

head: Result of the sundown healing
What followed
rows: Spread through Galilee, Judea, and beyond; Herod’s fears were aroused again and he sent watchers
From then on he became as much a physician as a preacher, while the apostles did most of the preaching and baptizing
Most were not permanently benefited spiritually; only a small number were truly edified
Much trouble from prejudice-raising publicity and unsought notoriety

p145.s4.b8: The narrator sums up: the healing wonders were not part of Jesus’ plan for proclaiming the kingdom but were incidental to having on earth a Creator with divine mercy and human sympathy. The observation that a remarkable experience does not by itself become spiritual growth is a check on any tendency to measure faith by the intensity of experience.
p145.s5.h: IV. The Evening After — The Apostles’ Elation and Jesus’ Absence
p145.s5.b0: That evening the apostles’ hopes rose higher than ever before. They believed they were seeing the fulfillment of Jesus’ promise that the hour had come for the kingdom to be proclaimed in power, and their lingering doubts about his divinity were banished. But Jesus was nowhere to be found. When he returned late, he refused their congratulations and adoration.

p145.s5.b1.q: Rejoice not that my Father is powerful to heal the body, but rather that he is mighty to save the soul.

p145.s5.b2: The apostles went to bed disappointed and perplexed; except for the twins, few of them slept much. Only one thought remained in their minds: “⟦Q 145:4.3⟧We cannot understand him.⟦/Q⟧”
p145.s6.h: V. Early Sunday Morning — Teaching Before Healing
p145.s6.b0: Jesus, too, slept little that night. He considered the danger that, in a world full of physical distress, caring for the sick would consume all his time and push the mission of establishing the spiritual kingdom into second place. Before daybreak he went out alone and prayed for wisdom and judgment, so that his human sympathy joined with his divine mercy would not crowd out his spiritual ministry. He did not wish to avoid ministering to the sick; he wished to protect the more important work of spiritual teaching.
p145.s6.b1: Peter, James, and John found him, and for more than four hours Jesus tried to explain why the kingdom could not be built on wonder-working and physical healing, but they could not comprehend. Then Andrew arrived, saying that all men were seeking him and urging him to come back. Jesus answered that the people were flocking to him because their bodies had been healed rather than because they had received spiritual truth.

p145.s6.b2.q: I have ordained you to preach the gospel and minister to the sick, but I must not become engrossed in healing to the exclusion of my teaching.

p145.s6.b3: And so, on the afternoon of Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles set out on their first public preaching tour of Galilee. The apostles regretted leaving, Peter reckoning that a thousand believers could have been baptized, until Thomas broke the silence.

p145.s6.b4.q: We follow a teacher who seeks no glory for himself.

p145.s6.b5: Shortly after they left for Rimmon, Jesus’ brothers James and Jude called at Zebedee’s house to see him, but he had already gone. On this first tour they preached in many cities but did not visit Nazareth. The apostles followed reluctantly, yet their steps led on into the wider field of Galilee.
p145.s7.b0: Paper 145 sets the most spectacular day of Jesus’ life side by side with one of his firmest decisions. People saw miracles even in coincidences, and even the genuine creative healing left most of its recipients without lasting spiritual benefit. At the very peak of popularity and expectation, Jesus walked away to return to his true mission: proclaiming the truth that saves the soul.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Stand before God as one person, not leaning only on a group’s faith
Work for a better world by first seeking your own enlightenment
Hope bound up in the progress of the individual (145:2.8)
Notice the fear beneath hatred and revenge
The shadow of fear, the mask of cowardice (145:3.4)
Rejoice more in the soul’s transformation than in remarkable experiences
Keep to your true mission even amid pressing needs
Not engrossed in healing to the exclusion of teaching (145:5.7)
Follow the Father’s will rather than popularity or results
A teacher who seeks no glory for himself (145:5.10)

p145.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 146, “First Preaching Tour of Galilee,” Jesus and the apostles carry the gospel of the kingdom to the cities of Galilee, beginning at Rimmon.
p146.lead: Two months on the first public preaching tour of Galilee: the discourse on prayer at Jotapata, the philosopher and the teaching on assurance at Ramah, the leper at Iron, and Jesus amid a wonder-seeking generation.

p146.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p146.s0.h: Introduction — The First Tour Without Restraint
p146.s0.b0: The first public preaching tour of Galilee began on Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, and lasted about two months, ending with the return to Capernaum on March 17. Jesus and the twelve, assisted by the former apostles of John, tarried, taught, and baptized believers in eleven cities.
p146.s0.b1: This was the first time Jesus permitted his associates to preach without restraint. He cautioned them only to stay away from Nazareth and to be discreet when passing through Capernaum and Tiberias, and the apostles threw themselves with great joy into preaching, ministering to the sick, and baptizing. Yet throughout, the paper also shows the steady tension between crowds expecting miracles and a Master wary of them.

head: Where they stayed
Main events
rows: Explaining how the gospel differs from older Babylonian and Persian beliefs; Todan hears the gospel
The discourse on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship
Conversation with a Greek philosopher; the teaching on assurance given to Thomas
Rare instruction on the social obligations of religion
Jesus works in the mines; the leper is cleansed
General rejection of the message; the apostles are discouraged
Titus’s son: foreknowledge of a natural process
The widow’s son, thought dead, is awakened
Rest from the crowds; teaching about spirits

p146.s1.h: I. Preaching at Rimmon — Old Beliefs and the New Gospel
p146.s1.b0: Rimmon had once been dedicated to Ramman, a Babylonian god of the air, and its people still held many Babylonian and Zoroastrian teachings. Jesus and the twenty-four therefore spent much time making plain the difference between these older beliefs and the gospel. Many became believers, but the narrator notes how hard it is to bring nature worshipers into full fellowship with a spiritual ideal within a single lifetime.
p146.s1.b1: The narrator explains that the better Babylonian and Persian ideas of light and darkness, good and evil, were later taken into Christian doctrine and made it more acceptable to the peoples of the Near East, just as Plato’s theories, adapted by Philo, eased the way for the western Greeks. Todan, who first heard the gospel at Rimmon, became one of the first to preach it beyond the Euphrates.
p146.s2.h: II. At Jotapata — Sixteen Teachings on Prayer
p146.s2.b0: On the second evening at Jotapata, Nathaniel, confused about the Master’s teaching on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship, asked for help, and Jesus explained at great length. The narrator summarizes the discourse in modern terms as sixteen points. Grouped by theme, their core runs as follows.

head: Theme
The heart of the teaching
rows: Conscious regard for iniquity; deliberate disdain for the laws of God
The Father has already forgiven, but in experience his forgiveness becomes real when we forgive others
Mercy cannot circumvent the basic law of justice; those who would receive mercy must show mercy
Prayer wholly dedicated to doing the Father’s will cannot remain unanswered
Less for self, more for the spiritual progress of others, especially those who curse and persecute us
Not only in trouble but also when all goes well; personal petitions in secret
Remaining receptive so the indwelling spirit may speak to the soul

p146.s2.b2.q: The sincerity of any prayer is the assurance of its being heard

p146.s2.b3: The time, manner, and degree of the answer are determined by the spiritual wisdom and universe consistency of the petition. A wise father does not literally grant the foolish requests of inexperienced children, though the children may find real soul satisfaction in making them. To be sure of being heard, then, is not the same as being sure of getting what we ask.

p146.s2.b4.q: Prayer does not change the divine attitude toward man, but it does change man’s attitude toward the changeless Father.

p146.s2.b5: Jesus taught that a thoroughly selfish soul cannot truly pray, and that prayer is no means of escaping the delays of time or the handicaps of space. Nor should we expect prayer for the sick to take the place of loving and intelligent ministry to their needs. Prayer does not replace action; it changes the one who acts.

p146.s2.b6.q: There is but one form of prayer which is appropriate for all God’s children, and that is: “Nevertheless, your will be done.”

p146.s2.b7: Jesus warned that ornate repetitions, fasting, penance, or sacrifices do not make prayer more effective, and he deplored how little of the spirit of thanksgiving was found in his followers’ prayers. He urged them to use prayer as a way of leading up through thanksgiving to true worship.

p146.s2.b8.q: Worship is a transforming experience whereby the finite gradually approaches and ultimately attains the presence of the Infinite.

p146.s3.h: III. The Stop at Ramah — The Philosopher and the Way of Assurance
p146.s3.b0: At Ramah Jesus listened with patience and sympathy to an aged Greek philosopher who held that science and philosophy were enough to satisfy human experience, and he granted the truth of much that the man said. Then he pointed out that the discussion had left out “⟦Q 146:3.1⟧whence, why, and whither,⟦/Q⟧” and that religion begins where philosophy leaves off. Sincerely honest of heart, the old philosopher soon believed the gospel.

p146.s3.b1.q: Where you leave off, we begin.

p146.s3.b2: When the apostles were disconcerted at seeing Jesus openly agree with the philosopher, he explained that truth does not fear honest criticism.

p146.s3.b3.q: intolerance is the mask covering up the entertainment of secret doubts as to the trueness of one’s belief

p146.s3.b4: Thomas asked how a new believer could really be certain of the truth of the gospel. Jesus answered that assurance is wholly a matter of personal experience and described it almost as a sum. He also gave a practical measure of how far one has yielded the soul to the indwelling spirit.

head: Spiritual assurance
What it involves
rows: The degree of one’s love for one’s fellow men
The Spirit of Truth, poured out on all flesh, will bear witness that we are sons of God

p146.s3.b6.q: He who enters the kingdom has eternal life already—he shall never perish.

p146.s3.b7: Since Jewish teaching had been confused about the survival of the righteous, these definite words about the eternal survival of believers were a great comfort. At this time each of Jesus’ apostles took one of John’s apostles as an associate. At Zebulun Jesus discussed the difference between personal religious experience and social religious obligations, one of the few times he did so, for he gave very little instruction about the socialization of religion.
p146.s4.h: IV. The Gospel at Iron — Among the Miners, and the Leper
p146.s4.b0: At this time every synagogue in Galilee and Judea was still open to Jesus. In the mining town of Iron, since he had never shared the life of a miner, he spent most of his time working underground with the laborers. He helped many of the sick, but he performed no so-called miracle of healing except for the leper.
p146.s4.b1: On the third day a leper knelt before him, believing he could not enter the kingdom unless he were made clean. Jesus’ human heart was touched, and the divine mind was moved with compassion.
p146.s4.b3: The narrator states that this was the first so-called miracle Jesus had deliberately performed, and that it was a case of real leprosy. But the man ignored the charge to tell no one and spread the news through the town, so that Jesus, thronged by the sick, had to leave early the next day. In Chorazin and Madon that followed, the message was largely rejected, and the apostles, blaming Jesus’ refusal to let them present him as a healer, longed for another display of power. The Master was unmoved.
p146.s5.h: V–VI. Back in Cana; Nain and the Widow’s Son — A Wonder-Seeking Generation
p146.s5.b0: At Cana, Titus, a prominent citizen of Capernaum, begged Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus lamented that except they see signs and wonders, people refuse to believe, then said, “⟦Q 146:5.2⟧Your son will live.⟦/Q⟧” The fever left the boy at that very hour, and Titus and his whole household believed. Yet the narrator explains that this was no miracle of curing physical disease, but a case of preknowledge of the course of natural law.
p146.s5.b1: At the gate of Nain Jesus met the funeral procession of a widow’s only son. Lifting the cover of the bier, he found that the young man was not really dead; he told the mother that her son was sleeping and then awakened him. Jesus tried again and again to explain that he had not raised the dead, but the people took his words as the modest way he always hid his miracles.

p146.s5.b2.q: Weep not. Your son is not dead; he sleeps. He will be restored to you.

head: Event
What people saw
What the narrator reveals
rows: The first so-called miracle done deliberately; real leprosy
A healing performed at a distance
Preknowledge of the course of natural law
Many with nervous and emotional disorders
A boy in a deep sleep, awakened

p146.s5.b4: The narrator sums it up: these people believed in signs; they were a wonder-seeking generation. Jesus could not make even all his apostles fully understand that the boy had not been dead, and whenever a rumor of miracles spread, he had to leave quickly. The section quietly warns that a heart hungry for the dramatic may close the ears that should be hearing the truth.
p146.s6.h: VII. At Endor — Teaching About Spirits
p146.s6.b0: At Endor, escaping the crowds for a few days, Jesus told the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor. He explained that the supposed spirits of the dead had been impersonated by stray and rebellious midwayers, and that after he returned to the Father and the spirit was poured out on all flesh, these so-called unclean spirits could no longer possess mortals. He also taught that the spirits of departed human beings do not come back to communicate with the living. After two days’ rest, Jesus proposed returning to Capernaum.
p146.s7.b0: Paper 146 holds together a widening ministry and a deepening teaching. The discourse at Jotapata shows that prayer is not a means of moving God but a process that brings us into line with the Father’s will; the conversation at Ramah shows that assurance is confirmed through experience and love. And amid a generation chasing wonders, Jesus kept truth ahead of signs to the end.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Before praying, set down the iniquity and resentment you are holding
When you ask forgiveness, forgive first
Do not let prayer replace practical love
Speak to the Father when all is well, too
After praying, wait in silence and listen
Giving the spirit opportunity to speak (146:2.17)
Hold convictions honest enough not to fear criticism
Intolerance is the mask of doubt (146:3.2)
Test your faith by how much you love others
The measure of yielding to the spirit (146:3.6)

p146.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 147, “The Interlude Visit to Jerusalem,” Jesus and the apostles pass through Capernaum and set out once more for Jerusalem.
p147.lead: The centurion’s faith, words of comfort at the pool of Bethesda, six levels of the golden rule, and the woman at Simon’s house: a record of the Passover visit to Jerusalem and the return to Galilee.

p147.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p147.s0.h: Introduction — Why Galilee Rather Than Jerusalem
p147.s0.b0: Jesus and the apostles returned to Capernaum on March 17 and spent two weeks at the Bethsaida headquarters. The apostles taught by the seaside, while Jesus spent much time alone in the hills and made two secret trips to Tiberias with James and John. There were a good many believers among the household of Herod.
p147.s0.b1: These believers explained to Herod that the kingdom was spiritual in nature and not a political venture, and Herod raised no objection to Jesus’ work. The narrator makes clear that the greatest danger to Jesus lay not in Herod but in the religious leaders at Jerusalem, which is why most of the public preaching took place in Galilee. This paper records the exceptional visit to Jerusalem, the “interlude.”
p147.s1.h: I. The Centurion’s Servant — The Faith of a Gentile
p147.s1.b0: On the day before the Passover journey, Mangus, a Roman centurion stationed at Capernaum, asked the rulers of the synagogue to request healing for his sick servant. The elders pleaded with Jesus, saying the centurion loved their nation and had even built their synagogue. As Jesus went with them, the centurion sent friends to say that he was not worthy to have the Master under his roof; Jesus need only speak the word.

p147.s1.b1.q: I marvel at the belief of the gentile. Verily, verily, I say to you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

p147.s1.b2: From that hour the servant began to mend and was eventually restored to health. Yet the narrator honestly adds that they never knew just what happened; whether invisible beings ministered healing was not revealed even to those who accompanied Jesus. The record stops at the fact of the servant’s complete recovery. This restraint, saying plainly what is not known, adds to the record’s trustworthiness.
p147.s2.h: II. The Journey to Jerusalem — A Quiet Passover
p147.s2.b0: Setting out on March 30, the party went by way of the Jordan valley and reached Bethany on April 2. Passing through Jericho, Judas deposited some of their common funds in the bank of a family friend, and that deposit was left undisturbed until their last journey to Jerusalem. Once at Bethany, they were so thronged by people seeking healing and comfort that they pitched tents at Gethsemane.

head: Item
What the record says
rows: No public preaching, only private teaching and personal work
Celebrated quietly at Bethany—the first bloodless Passover shared by Jesus and all the twelve
Celebrated separately with Abner, then remained to labor in and around Jerusalem
Differences of opinion, yet co-operation and the best of feelings

p147.s2.b2: The twenty-four were not all together again until shortly before the seventy were commissioned. That the two groups nonetheless co-operated shows that workers with different methods can labor under one purpose.
p147.s3.h: III. At the Pool of Bethesda — Words of Comfort Instead of a Miracle
p147.s3.b0: On a Sabbath afternoon John, the youngest apostle, led Jesus to the pool of Bethesda. Its reddish-tinged hot spring bubbled up at intervals because of gas in the caverns beneath, and people believed that the first to enter the water afterward would be healed. John hoped that the sight of so many sufferers would move the Master to work a miracle, and that all Jerusalem would then believe the gospel.

p147.s3.b1.q: John, why would you tempt me to turn aside from the way I have chosen?

p147.s3.b2: Instead of a miracle, Jesus gathered the sick and spoke words of good cheer. Suffering has many causes: years of wrong living, the accidents of time, the mistakes of forebears, the imperfect conditions of temporal existence. But, he said, it is even greater to be cleansed of spiritual disease and healed of moral infirmity than to be freed from bodily affliction, and as God’s children they would all find not only justice but an abundance of mercy.

p147.s3.b3.q: You are all God’s children; you are the sons of the heavenly Father. The bonds of time may seem to afflict you, but the God of eternity loves you.

p147.s3.b4: Many who heard believed the gospel, and some were so spiritually revived that they went about proclaiming they had been cured of their physical ailments as well. Jesus left before the chief priests could take offense, and John never told the other apostles about the visit. The miracle he had hoped for did not come; what he saw instead was the power of words to raise people up.
p147.s3.b5: One man had waited for years for someone to help him and had never once entertained the idea of helping himself. Gladdened by Jesus’ words, he took up his bed and went home. The narrator explains that taking up his bed and walking was the one thing he had to do in order to recover. The scene shows that what a person trapped in helplessness needs is sometimes not an outward miracle but an inward rising.
p147.s4.h: IV. The Rule of Living — Six Levels of the Golden Rule
p147.s4.b0: That evening Nathaniel asked what happens when a man with evil desires twists the rule of doing to others as we would have them do to us. Jesus answered that he had spoken to men of high ideals, and, disappointed that they so often failed to give his plain teachings a spiritual interpretation, he taught them the levels at which the rule may be understood.

head: Level
How the rule is interpreted
rows: A purely selfish and lustful interpretation
Sympathy and pity enhance the interpretation
The reason of mind and the intelligence of experience; the highest idealism of profound self-respect
Unselfish devotion to the welfare of one’s fellows, growing out of the consciousness of the fatherhood of God
Viewing the problem as a wise and impartial third person would
The divine command to treat all men as we conceive God would treat them

p147.s4.b2.q: I would, therefore, that you should do to all men that which you know I would do to them in like circumstances.

p147.s4.b3: The narrator notes that nothing Jesus had said up to that time had ever more astonished the apostles. The same sentence becomes an entirely different rule depending on the level at which it is read. Readers can ask themselves at which level they are actually practicing the golden rule.
p147.s5.h: V. Visiting Simon the Pharisee — The Love of One Forgiven Much
p147.s5.b0: Simon, a Pharisee and a halfhearted believer, invited Jesus and three apostles to a meal. By custom the doors were left open, and among those who came in from the street was a woman who had believed the gospel and closed her brothel. She anointed Jesus’ feet with perfumed lotion, wet them with her tears of gratitude, and wiped them with her hair.
p147.s5.b1: When Simon silently judged her a sinner, Jesus answered with the story of two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty. Then he pointed out, one by one, how the woman had supplied the hospitality Simon had neglected.

p147.s5.b2.q: Simply that her many sins have been forgiven, and this has led her to love much.

p147.s5.b3.q: You have indeed repented of your sins, and they are forgiven. Be not discouraged by the thoughtless and unkind attitude of your fellows; go on in the joy and liberty of the kingdom of heaven.

p147.s5.b4: As he left, Jesus told Simon that he knew how he was torn between faith and doubts, distraught by fear and troubled by pride. And he declared that no one can close the doors of the kingdom even to the most flagrant sinner on earth, if such a one sincerely seeks entrance.
p147.s6.h: V (continued). The Evening Address — Direction Over Status
p147.s6.b0: That evening Jesus spoke on the relative value of status with God and progress in the eternal ascent. Humanly speaking, the transformed woman stood on a level far below Simon’s, yet her soul was in progressive motion; the Pharisees, meanwhile, were caught in the false progress of meaningless ceremonial circles.

p147.s6.b1.q: What you are becoming day by day is of infinitely more importance than what you are today.

head: What matters
What matters less
rows: What you are becoming day by day
A small but living and growing faith
A great intellect with its dead stores of worldly wisdom and spiritual unbelief

p147.s6.b3: At the same time Jesus warned against the folly of presuming on the Father’s love. The heavenly Father is not a lax, indulgent parent ready to condone sin, and he does not tolerate self-destructive acts that ruin moral growth. Jesus thus kept his emphasis on direction from becoming an excuse for license.
p147.s7.h: VI. Returning to Capernaum — The Spies and the Sabbath
p147.s7.b0: The leaders at Jerusalem decided that Jesus must be tried by the Sanhedrin on a religious charge and appointed six secret spies, who joined the party at Jericho under the pretense of wanting to become disciples. When Jesus set out on the Sabbath, the spies thought they had their charge, but Jesus instructed Andrew to go only one thousand yards, the legal Sabbath day’s journey.
p147.s7.b1: As they passed through the wheat fields, some apostles rubbed out grain and ate it, and the spies protested that this broke the Sabbath. Jesus acknowledged their zeal but said it would be better to guard the health and well-being of their fellows.

p147.s7.b2.q: I declare that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath.

p147.s7.b3: The narrator observes that Jesus’ antagonism to tradition and ceremonial was always positive: it consisted in what he did and what he affirmed, and he spent little time in negative denunciation. Showing a better way rather than criticizing remains a sound approach for readers today.
p147.s8.h: VII–VIII. Back in Capernaum; The Feast of Spiritual Goodness
p147.s8.b0: On May 3 the party came by boat to Bethsaida to escape the crowds, but by the next day many, the spies included, had found Jesus again. At a question-and-answer session the leader of the spies asked why he never commanded his disciples to fast. Jesus answered with John’s saying that the sons of the bridechamber do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, and with the parable of new wine in fresh wine skins: prayer is natural for the children of light, but fasting is not part of the gospel of the kingdom.

head: What we meet
How to respond
rows: What is old and also true
What is new and also true
Have the faith and courage to accept it

p147.s8.b2: That night Jesus quoted Isaiah to teach the true fast: not afflicting one’s soul, but loosing the bonds of wickedness, letting the oppressed go free, and sharing bread with the hungry. Until after two in the morning he explained that what made them secure in the kingdom was faith, not affliction of soul or fasting of body.

p147.s8.b3.q: Grow in grace by means of that living faith which grasps the fact that you are the sons of God while at the same time it recognizes every man as a brother.

p147.s9.b0: Paper 147 gathers many scenes into a short visit to Jerusalem, but one current runs beneath them all. Jesus chose words of comfort over miracles, levels of interpretation over the letter of a rule, the direction of progress over present status, and service over formal fasting. Every one of these choices aimed to set people not under the law but within a living faith.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Try applying the golden rule one level higher
In helplessness, find the one thing you can do yourself
Taking up the bed and walking (147:3.5)
See where others are heading, not only where they stand
Never make love an excuse for license
Show a better way rather than denouncing
Find the courage to accept what is new and true
New wine in fresh wine skins (147:7.3)

p147.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 148, “Training Evangelists at Bethsaida,” Jesus trains new evangelists at the seaside headquarters.
p148.lead: Five months by the sea at Bethsaida: a school for evangelists and the kingdom’s first hospital, the distinction between evil, sin, and iniquity, and the discourse on suffering and Job.

p148.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p148.s0.h: Introduction — The Most Organized Five Months
p148.s0.b0: From May 3 to October 3, A.D. 28, Jesus and the apostles lived at the Zebedee home in Bethsaida. By the seaside nearby rose a tented city of five hundred to fifteen hundred people, under the general supervision of David Zebedee. The camp was a model of order and sanitation, and the sick were cared for separately under a Syrian physician named Elman.
p148.s0.b1: The narrator calls this the longest settled and best-organized period of the Master’s teaching. Several thousand came and went, from every part of the Roman Empire and from lands east of the Euphrates. This paper records the school and hospital founded in those five months, and the deep conversations held in the garden.

head: Role
Who
How it worked
rows: Directed the apostles’ work as a whole
Group teaching in the forenoon; teachers and pupils taught the people in the afternoon
David Zebedee, with the Alpheus twins
Run as a self-sustaining enterprise; no one was ever turned away
The sick of different types were segregated and supervised
The apostles; Jesus once a week
Five nights a week after supper; Jesus answered the holdover questions

p148.s1.h: I. A New School of the Prophets — Learning and Doing
p148.s1.b0: Peter, James, and Andrew passed on applicants, and the students represented the peoples of the Roman world and the East as far as India. The school was run on the plan of learning and doing: what the students learned in the morning they taught by the seaside in the afternoon, and in the evening they discussed both together.
p148.s1.b1: Most striking is that the teaching was not made uniform. Each apostle presented his own interpretation of the gospel, and Jesus upheld this diversity, harmonizing the various views at his weekly question hours.

p148.s1.b2.q: They made no effort to teach just alike; there was no standardized or dogmatic formulation of theologic doctrines.

p148.s1.b3: The hundred and more evangelists trained here became the material from which the later seventy were drawn. Allowing the same truth to be told in the language of different experiences reminds faith communities today of the worth of living diversity over uniformity.
p148.s2.h: II. The Bethsaida Hospital — Healing Without Miracles
p148.s2.b0: With a corps of twenty-five young women and twelve men, Elman ran for four months what should be regarded as the kingdom’s first hospital. They treated the sick by all known material methods together with the spiritual practices of prayer and faith encouragement. Jesus visited at least three times a week and made personal contact with each sufferer.

p148.s2.b1.q: As far as we know, no so-called miracles of supernatural healing occurred among the one thousand afflicted and ailing persons who went away from this infirmary improved or cured.

p148.s2.b2: Even so, the patients kept saying that Jesus had healed them. The narrator explains that these were transformations of mind and spirit in expectant, faith-filled people under the influence of a strong and beneficent personality whose ministry banished fear and anxiety. It is an insight that healing happens when medicine, faith, and personal care work together.
p148.s2.b3: Elman and his associates tried to correct the near-universal belief that sickness was caused by unclean spirits, with little success. Jesus himself did not reveal techniques of treatment or the unknown causes of disease, keeping to the instructions Immanuel had given him before the incarnation. Still, those caring for the sick learned much by watching how he inspired faith and confidence in the suffering.
p148.s3.h: III. The Father’s Business — Time Alone
p148.s3.b0: During this period Jesus led public services fewer than a dozen times, and not since his baptism had he been so much alone. Asked why he was so often absent, he always answered that he was “⟦Q 148:3.2⟧about the Father’s business.⟦/Q⟧” Each time he took along any two apostles who were free, so that all twelve had the chance of close association with him.
p148.s3.b1: The narrator infers that during these hours Jesus was in direct association with his chief directors of universe affairs. This is offered only as an inference: the apostles nearby saw his features change rapidly but heard no words and saw no celestial beings. That the busiest season, with crowds pressing in, was also the season of his longest solitude suggests that the depth of outward work comes from quiet hours.
p148.s4.h: IV. Evil, Sin, and Iniquity — Thomas’s Question
p148.s4.b0: Thomas asked why one must be born again and what evil is. Jesus first warned him not to confuse evil with “⟦Q 148:4.2⟧the evil one,⟦/Q⟧” the high administrator who went into deliberate rebellion. Then he distinguished three concepts by their relation to the Father’s will.

head: Concept
How the Father’s will is transgressed
What it measures
rows: Continued rejection of the plan of survival and the ministry of salvation

p148.s4.b2.q: Men are, indeed, by nature evil, but not necessarily sinful.

p148.s4.b3.q: Evil is inherent in the natural order of this world, but sin is an attitude of conscious rebellion which was brought to this world by those who fell from spiritual light into gross darkness.

p148.s4.b4: Jesus pointed out that Thomas was confused by the idea that mankind fell from a perfect state. Man is not descending toward destruction; by entering the kingdom he is ascending to divine perfection. Imperfection of natural endowment is not sin, nor does it make man an estranged stepchild of the Father. This distinction gives an accurate self-understanding back to anyone weighed down by guilt over his or her shortcomings.
p148.s5.h: V. The Purpose of Affliction — Nathaniel’s Question
p148.s5.b0: Nathaniel asked why a loving Father permits his children to suffer so many afflictions. Jesus explained that the natural order of this world has been upset many times by the sinful adventures of rebels, and that setting things right will take many ages.

p148.s5.b1.q: But of one thing you may be sure: The Father does not send affliction as an arbitrary punishment for wrongdoing.

p148.s5.b2: The imperfections of evil are inherent, the penalties of sin inevitable, and the destroying consequences of iniquity inexorable. We should not, then, blame God for the natural results of the life we choose. It is the Father’s will that we work persistently to better our estate, and intelligent application can overcome much earthly misery. We should also drop the habit of laying on God everything we fail to understand.
p148.s6.h: VI. The Misunderstanding of Suffering — Discourse on Job
p148.s6.b0: That same evening John asked about the suffering of the apparently innocent, and Jesus answered through the story of Job. He first corrected the time-honored notion that material prosperity is evidence of divine favor: the Father loves the poor just as much as the rich. Men do reap what they sow, but not all suffering is punishment for past sin.

head: Figure
The position taken
Jesus’ assessment
rows: Only the wicked suffer, so you must deserve this punishment
A false comforter; Job got little comfort from him
Your children perished, so they must have been sinners
Sound by the theology of the day, but even more depressing
Perhaps there is some hidden purpose in your miseries
Appeals to a just God and longs for a human God
Altogether right to challenge the doctrine that God punishes children for their parents

p148.s6.b2: Job found no philosophical answer, but after a great struggle between faith and doubt he began to see the light of life. Jesus said that it was his mission to show the human God Job longed for, a divine Being who knows man’s mortal estate. The Father does not speak from the whirlwind but within the human heart as a still, small voice.

head: Source of suffering
Jesus’ explanation
rows: The accidents of time and the imperfections of the evil of an immature physical existence
The inexorable consequences of sin, the transgression of the laws of life and light
The harvest of persistent rebellion against the righteous rule of heaven
A personal visitation of divine judgment

p148.s6.b4.q: The Father in heaven does not willingly afflict the children of men.

p148.s6.b5.q: Do you not comprehend that God dwells within you, that he has become what you are that he may make you what he is!

p148.s6.b6: John pondered these sayings for many days, and his whole later life was changed by them. In later times he did much to help the other apostles change their views about the source and purpose of human afflictions.
p148.s7.h: VII. The Man with the Withered Hand — Doing Good on the Sabbath
p148.s7.b0: On a Sabbath before the second tour, the leader of the spies induced a man with a withered hand to ask whether it was lawful to be healed on the Sabbath. Jesus asked whether one would lift a sheep out of a pit on the Sabbath, and, declaring how much more valuable a man is than a sheep, proclaimed it lawful to do good. When the man stretched out his hand, it was made whole.

p148.s7.b1.q: I proclaim that it is lawful to do good to men on the Sabbath day.

p148.s7.b2: The narrator explains that this was the first miracle Jesus performed in response to his enemies’ challenge, done not as a display of power but as a protest against turning the Sabbath into a bondage of meaningless restrictions. When the people were minded to turn on the Pharisees, Jesus calmed them: permission to do good is no license to do harm.
p148.s8.h: VIII–IX. Last Week at Bethsaida; Healing the Paralytic — The Camp Disbands
p148.s8.b0: Much happened in the last week. Abraham, a young member of the Sanhedrin, was baptized by Abner and gave his goods to the apostolic treasury, helping to send out the evangelists. An invitation from Alexandria was courteously declined. Jesus allowed Kirmeth, a self-styled trance prophet from Bagdad, freedom to speak for a few days, and the people soon recognized for themselves that his teaching was unsound.
p148.s8.b1: During the final meeting on October 1, a paralytic from Capernaum had his friends loosen the roof tiles and lower him on his couch before Jesus. He said he wished to be made whole in order to serve in the kingdom. Seeing his faith, Jesus declared his sins forgiven, and before those who called this blasphemy he told the man to rise, take up his bed, and go home.

p148.s8.b2.q: I would be made whole that I might serve in the kingdom of heaven.

p148.s8.b3: Just then messengers came summoning the spies back to the Sanhedrin. Their leader and two others returned, but the other three Pharisees confessed faith in Jesus and were baptized by Peter. Even among those sent to watch, some opened their hearts to the truth.
p148.s9.b0: At the heart of Paper 148 is a corrected way of seeing suffering. God does not send affliction as punishment, and we are not stepchildren estranged from the Father because of our shortcomings. The paper also offers practical models: teaching without uniformity, healing joined with personal care, and time spent alone with the Father.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Put what you learn into practice right away
A school of learning and doing (148:1.1)
Respect fellow believers who interpret differently
See yourself truly by telling imperfection from sin
Do not assume suffering is God’s punishment
Offer the suffering comfort, not judgment

p148.s9.b2: In the next paper, Paper 149, “⟦Q 148:7.1⟧The Second Preaching Tour⟦/Q⟧,” Jesus and the apostles set out into Galilee with the newly trained evangelists.
p149.lead: Three months touring Galilee with 117 evangelists: unconscious healings, the attraction and balanced character of Jesus, contentment, and a new reading of “the fear of the Lord.”

p149.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p149.s0.h: Introduction — A Training Tour for the Evangelists
p149.s0.b0: The second preaching tour of Galilee began on October 3, A.D. 28, and ended on December 30. Jesus, the twelve, and a newly recruited corps of 117 evangelists visited Gadara, Ptolemais, Megiddo, Scythopolis, and many other cities. The narrator explains that the whole tour was principally an effort to give the new evangelists practical experience.
p149.s0.b1: Asked to give the final charge before departure, Jesus declined, saying it was not his province to do what others could acceptably perform, and James Zebedee gave the charge instead. Handing over what can be handed over is the way of a leader who develops people.

head: Role
What the record says
rows: Traveled with James and John, often visiting two cities a day to observe and encourage the evangelists
Each took about a dozen evangelists and baptized believers
Preached and taught, gaining practical experience
Ran a clearinghouse at the Bethsaida headquarters with forty to fifty messengers

p149.s1.h: I. The Widespread Fame of Jesus — Unconscious Healing
p149.s1.b0: By now Jesus’ fame as a healer had spread through all of Palestine and Syria. On this tour he did not deliberately perform any so-called miracles, yet more than a hundred people were beneficiaries of his unconscious healing. He told them to “⟦Q 149:1.2⟧tell no man⟦/Q⟧,” but they went home and spread his fame still further.

p149.s1.b1.q: The Master never explained to his apostles how these healings were effected, other than that on several occasions he merely said, “I perceive that power has gone forth from me.”

p149.s1.b2: Offering it expressly as an opinion, the narrator explains that such healings came about when three associated influences were present together.

head: Influence
What it involves
rows: Strong, living faith that persistently sought healing, desired for its spiritual benefits more than for physical restoration
The great sympathy and compassion of the mercy-dominated Creator Son, with almost unlimited healing powers
If the Father did not will otherwise, the need and the power became one, and healing occurred

p149.s1.b4: The narrator therefore believes that, in Jesus’ presence, profound human faith literally compelled the creative forces and personalities of the universe to manifest healing. By the record, Jesus often allowed people to heal themselves in his presence by their powerful personal faith. Worth noticing is that the initiative in healing lay partly with the faith of the one receiving it.
p149.s1.b5: By contrast, a rich widow of Tyre followed Jesus around offering more and more money, with no interest in the gospel. Treating God’s power as something the highest bidder could buy, she shows clearly the difference between faith and selfish desire.
p149.s2.h: II. Attitude of the People — What Was Added to the Gospel
p149.s2.b0: The narrator says that, had Jesus’ teachings been left as he presented them, all nations and religions would soon have embraced them. The well-meant efforts of his early followers to restate the teachings for particular groups only made them less acceptable to everyone else. So Christianity contains more of the Master’s gospel than any other religion, yet also much that Jesus did not teach.

head: Two great mistakes
The narrator’s explanation
rows: 1. Tying the gospel directly to Jewish theology
The doctrine of the atonement—a sacrificed Son satisfying the Father’s stern justice and appeasing divine wrath—confused and alienated many honest souls
2. Organizing the teaching around the person of Jesus
Overemphasis on his personality obscured his teachings and made them harder for Eastern religionists to accept

p149.s2.b2.q: Learn to approach the miracle through Jesus, but do not make the mistake of approaching Jesus through the miracle.

p149.s2.b3: The narrator advises approaching other religions by recognizing the truths held in common rather than stressing differences. He calls Jesus’ attitude toward women, taking them along as teachers of the gospel, the most revolutionary feature of his mission, and the one shameful thing about the religion bearing his name that it lacked the courage to follow this example.
p149.s2.b4: Jesus was free from superstition and prejudice, and he dared to teach that natural catastrophes are not divine judgments. Yet he was no militant revolutionary; he tore down what was only when he could offer at the same time the better thing that ought to be.

p149.s2.b5.q: He was not a militant revolutionist; he was a progressive evolutionist.

p149.s2.b6: His fame at first rested on healing, but more and more people sought him for spiritual help: victims of moral enslavement, fathers asking about their sons, mothers about their daughters, and he always helped them. He did not exact obedience and was never dictatorial, yet he commanded confidence. Only those who had not met him feared him.

p149.s2.b7.q: And the better they knew him the more they loved him.

p149.s3.h: III. Hostility of the Religious Leaders — Closed Hearts
p149.s3.b0: While the common people received Jesus gladly, the leaders at Jerusalem were becoming well-nigh frantic over young Abraham’s conversion and the desertion of three of the spies. The Pharisees had built a systematic theology, whereas Jesus taught as occasion served, in parables. The narrator adds that each parable was meant to illustrate a single feature, and that many wrong ideas come from turning the parables into allegories.

p149.s3.b1.q: The only uniform thing about men is the indwelling spirit.

p149.s3.b2: Jesus taught that only through appeal to this spirit can mankind attain unity and brotherhood. But when men shut off the spirit’s appeal, little can be done to change their attitude. From this time on the leaders never ceased plotting, convinced that Jesus must be executed as a religious offender.
p149.s4.h: IV. Progress of the Preaching Tour — Anger and a Balanced Character
p149.s4.b0: When a young evangelist asked about anger, Jesus said that it measures the failure of the spiritual nature to control the intellectual and physical natures. Anger shows a lack of tolerant brotherly love and of self-control; it depletes the health and handicaps the spirit teacher of the soul. He urged them to let their hearts be dominated by love.

head: Virtue
Danger when carried too far
The balance Jesus asked for
rows: Avoiding the dullness of overconservative mediocrity
Piety without sanctimoniousness; reverence free from fear and superstition

p149.s4.b2: What impressed his associates was less the teaching than a life that exemplified it. He never wavered amid stress and storm, and even when his enemies used every unfair method, he never resorted to ignoble tactics. The narrator adds that, though most must specialize to earn a living, it is wholly desirable to cultivate a wide familiarity with life as others live it.
p149.s5.h: V. Lesson Regarding Contentment — The Vale of Soul Making
p149.s5.b0: When Simon Zelotes asked why some people are happier than others, Jesus answered that much depends on one’s willingness to be led by the Father’s indwelling spirit. Much human sorrow comes from disappointed ambition, wounded pride, and fear. Having sincerely done our best, we should cheerfully accept our lot and use ingenuity in making the most of it.

p149.s5.b1.q: Seek not, then, for false peace and transient joy but rather for the assurance of faith and the sureties of divine sonship

p149.s5.b2: Jesus hardly regarded this world as a “⟦Q 149:5.5⟧vale of tears.⟦/Q⟧” To him it was the birth sphere of eternal spirits, the “⟦Q 149:5.5⟧vale of soul making.⟦/Q⟧” The same reality yields more or less contentment depending on how we see it. Rereading a painful day as a time when the soul is growing is the practical use of this teaching.
p149.s6.h: VI. The “Fear of the Lord” — From Fear to Love
p149.s6.b0: At Gamala Philip asked how to reconcile the Scripture’s command to “⟦Q 149:6.1⟧fear the Lord⟦/Q⟧” with Jesus’ teaching to look to the Father without fear. Jesus explained that the phrase had meant different things in successive ages, and that his mission was to lead men up from reverence to love.

head: Stage
Attitude toward God
rows: Fear → anguish and dread → awe and reverence
Reverence → recognition, realization, and appreciation → love
Fear God and keep his commandments
Love God and learn to do his will

p149.s6.b2.q: The goodness of God leads to repentance; the beneficence of God leads to service; the mercy of God leads to salvation; while the love of God leads to intelligent and freehearted worship.

p149.s6.b3: Jesus said the kingdom has no high and mighty king; it is a divine family. He pointed out that false humility and hypocrisy grow out of wrong ideas of God. Humility before God belongs in the depths of the heart, but attention-craving humility is childish, for there is a divine dignity in those whom the spirit indwells.

p149.s6.b4.q: You do well to be meek before God and self-controlled before men

p149.s6.b5: Jesus also explained why he so often used the little child as an example: not for innocence, but to stress sincerity and perfect trust in the heavenly Father’s love and guidance. And he recalled the prophets’ warnings against being near God in the mouth but far from him in the heart, flattering with the lips while the heart is given to double-dealing.
p149.s7.h: VII. Returning to Bethsaida — The Test of Experience
p149.s7.b0: On the rainy evening of December 30 all the apostles and evangelists gathered at Zebedee’s house. Even the older teachers were edified by the young preachers’ accounts of their experiences. Yet of the 117 evangelists, only about seventy-five survived the test of actual experience and were ready for further service. During the two-week recess Jesus conferred with four apostles about extending the kingdom.
p149.s7.b1: The record states plainly that more than a third of those trained did not remain. Learning is tested in real experience, and those who pass the test become the workers of the next stage. That is exactly why the evangelists were sent into the field on this tour.
p149.s8.b0: Paper 149 shows what happens when the gospel passes through human hands: unconscious healings and fame, doctrines added along the way, closed hearts, and workers who pass the test. In the midst of it all, Jesus taught and lived a balanced character and a relationship with God that is love without fear.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Approach faith through Jesus, not through miracles
Look first for the truths you share with other faiths
When anger rises, let love take charge of your heart
Watch that your strengths do not run to extremes
Any virtue carried to extremes may become a vice (149:4.3)
Having done your best, accept your lot and live creatively
Relate to God in love rather than fear

p149.s8.b2: In the next paper, Paper 150, “The Third Preaching Tour,” the women’s evangelistic corps is organized, and Jesus sends the apostles out two by two through Galilee once more.
p150.lead: The commissioning of the women’s corps, a talk on superstition, apostles sent out two by two, the question of salvation, and rejection in his hometown of Nazareth: the third preaching tour of Galilee.

p150.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p150.s0.h: Introduction — Seven Weeks, the Last Round of Galilee
p150.s0.b0: In January of A.D. 29, Abner and the apostles of John, whose headquarters were at Hebron, came to Bethsaida for a joint conference with Jesus’ apostles. John’s apostles proposed making the anointing of the sick with oil a uniform practice for both groups, but Jesus’ apostles refused to bind themselves by such a regulation, and Jesus declined to take part in the discussion. A difference of practice was not settled by a rule.
p150.s0.b1: On January 18 the twenty-four, joined by about seventy-five tested evangelists, set out on the third preaching tour. The evangelists went in groups of five, and the apostles went out two and two to baptize as occasion required. For seven weeks they covered Magdala, Tiberias, Nazareth, and the cities of central and southern Galilee; except for the northern parts, this was their last message to Galilee.
p150.s1.h: I. The Women’s Evangelistic Corps — A Proclamation of Emancipation
p150.s1.b0: The narrator says that of all the daring things Jesus did, the most amazing was his sudden announcement on the evening of January 16 that the next day ten women would be set apart for the work of the kingdom. These women had served in the former encampment and the tented infirmary, and neither they nor their teachers had imagined that women would be commissioned to teach the gospel.

p150.s1.b1.q: On the morrow we will set apart ten women for the ministering work of the kingdom.

head: Name
Who she was
rows: Daughter of the former chazan of the Nazareth synagogue; elected chief
Wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod Antipas; elected treasurer
Daughter of a wealthy Jew of Tiberias and Sepphoris
Elder sister of Andrew and Peter
Sister-in-law of Jude, the Master’s brother in the flesh
Daughter of Elman, the Syrian physician
Mary Magdalene, and Rebecca, the daughter of Joseph of Arimathea

p150.s1.b3: The women organized themselves and, after the first funds for equipment, provided their own support. In an age when women were confined to the synagogue gallery, their commissioning stunned even the twelve. The narrator calls Jesus’ charge to them an emancipation proclamation for all women and for all time, while recording that later generations fell back into the old customs.

p150.s1.b4.q: no more was man to look upon woman as his spiritual inferior

p150.s1.b5: The whole country was stirred and Jesus’ enemies made great capital of it, but women believers everywhere stood stanchly behind their chosen sisters. In the early church, the narrator says, women teachers and ministers were called deaconesses and given general recognition. Paul, however, though he conceded all this in theory, never really made it part of his own attitude. The passage shows the gap between knowing a principle and living it.
p150.s2.h: II. The Stop at Magdala — The Fruit of the Women’s Ministry
p150.s2.b0: With the women’s corps in place, women believers could far more easily confer with Jesus or the apostles. At Magdala the wisdom of the choice was first demonstrated. The apostles were bound by strict rules about personal work with women of questionable character, but the women evangelists could freely enter the evil resorts, preach the glad tidings directly, and draw close to their afflicted sisters.
p150.s2.b1: As a result, Mary Magdalene was won for the kingdom. The narrator explains that a succession of misfortunes and the attitude of reputable society had brought her to one of Magdala’s resorts. Martha and Rachel made plain to her that the doors of the kingdom were open even to her, and she was baptized the next day. She became the most effective gospel teacher among the twelve women.

p150.s2.b2.q: notwithstanding the apostles all fled but one, these women were all present, and not one either denied or betrayed him

p150.s3.h: III. Sabbath at Tiberias — Magic and Superstition
p150.s3.b0: At Jesus’ direction the Sabbath service was placed in the women’s hands, and Joanna led it in the banquet room of Herod’s new palace. That evening, when Andrew asked whether a bright new star signified the birth of a great man, Jesus entered on a thoroughgoing discussion of human superstition, which the narrator summarizes in modern terms.

head: Superstition
Jesus’ teaching
rows: The courses of the stars have nothing to do with human life; astronomy is proper science, astrology superstitious error
Reveals nothing about weather or future events
The spirits of the dead do not come back to communicate with family or friends
Impotent to heal disease or ward off disaster
Convenient for minor matters, but no method of disclosing the divine will
Largely a superstitious and fantastic system of speculation
Nothing more than the material of which they are made

p150.s3.b2.q: The only means of communion with the spiritual world is embraced in the spirit endowment of mankind, the indwelling spirit of the Father, together with the outpoured spirit of the Son and the omnipresent influence of the Infinite Spirit.

p150.s3.b3: The heart of this talk is to give up every attempt to move the spiritual world by material means. The urge to lean on omens and luck in anxious times is common even today. Jesus teaches us to fill that place with a direct relationship with the indwelling spirit.
p150.s4.h: IV. Sending the Apostles out Two and Two — Fear Not
p150.s4.b0: Saying that the harvest was plenteous but the laborers few, Jesus kept the younger teachers with him and sent the apostles out in pairs to pass quickly through Galilee. This time they were not to go to gentile cities or Samaria, but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, proclaiming the saving truth that man is a son of God.

p150.s4.b2.q: Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than a great many sparrows.

p150.s4.b3: Jesus warned them in advance that peace would not always attend their preaching. When only part of a family receives the gospel, division and sorrow can follow, so they were to labor to save the whole family. It was a sending-forth that joined comfort with realistic warning.
p150.s5.h: V–VI. What Must I Do to Be Saved? — Salvation as a Gift; The Evening Lessons
p150.s5.b0: At Shunem Rachel asked how to answer women who ask what they must do to be saved. Jesus’ answer was simple: believe the gospel, accept divine forgiveness, and by faith recognize the indwelling spirit of God. Entrance into the kingdom is wholly free, but growth in grace is essential to continuing in it.

p150.s5.b1.q: You cannot buy salvation; you cannot earn righteousness.

head: Common idea
Jesus’ teaching
rows: We are saved by living righteously
We live righteously because we have already been saved and have recognized sonship
Righteousness is a merit earned by effort
Righteousness is the natural fruit of the spirit-born life
Repentance is demanded as a condition
Believing in God’s goodness leads to voluntary repentance
Once saved, the matter is finished
By faith we are eternally advanced toward divine perfection

p150.s5.b3: The women rejoiced all the more to know they were included in the plans for the kingdom. In the evening lessons that followed, Jesus spoke on many subjects—the love of God, dreams and visions, humility and meekness, music and worship, doubts and unbelief—and with the older apostles away, the younger men and women joined the discussions more freely.
p150.s5.b4: Jesus moved from group to group, spending two or three days with each, and knew where all the workers were through David’s messengers. News from the other groups was always a source of encouragement to the scattered workers. That news of one another strengthens those who labor far apart holds just as true for communities today.
p150.s6.h: VII–VIII. The Sojourn at Nazareth; The Sabbath Service
p150.s6.b0: On March 4 all the groups gathered at Nazareth, Jesus’ first visit since beginning his public ministry. Unrecognized, he walked past his childhood home and the carpenter shop, and not since his baptism had such a flood of human emotion stirred within him. But the town was hostile. There was resentment and jealousy that he had done no great works there, and his enemies had hired rough men to make trouble.
p150.s6.b1: In the synagogue on the Sabbath Jesus was handed the very scroll he had once presented to it, and he read from Deuteronomy and Isaiah: the word of life is not in heaven or beyond the sea but near, in one’s heart. Saying, “⟦Q 150:8.10⟧Today are these Scriptures fulfilled⟦/Q⟧,” he spoke on the sons and daughters of God, and many marveled at his graciousness.
